hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed heart of Lamu, a maze of narrow coral-stone lanes lined with carved wooden doors and centuries-old houses; the essential base for any visit.
A short walk or donkey ride from Lamu town, a quieter village with a long beach and Lamu's most upscale guesthouses.
The bustling dhow-lined harbor where boats arrive and depart, lined with cafes and a good spot to watch daily island life.
A remote, sparsely populated stretch on the island's southern tip, reached by boat, offering total quiet and mangrove scenery.
A neighboring island reached by dhow, home to the Takwa ruins and quieter beaches than Lamu's own.

water.note: Drink bottled water; island wells are brackish and untreated.

landmarks: Lamu Old Town
East Africa's oldest and best-preserved Swahili settlement, a UNESCO-listed maze of coral-stone houses, carved doors and donkey-width lanes founded in the 14th century.
Lamu Fort
A massive early-19th-century Omani fortress dominating the main square, now hosting a library, environmental museum and community events.
Lamu Museum
The waterfront museum on the seafront telling the archipelago's Swahili story through dhow models, ceremonial siwa horns and ethnographic treasures.
Shela Beach
Twelve kilometers of empty, dune-backed golden sand beginning at Shela village, arguably Kenya's most beautiful and unspoiled beach.
Shela Village
An impossibly chic yet timeless village of whitewashed mansions, boutique guesthouses and the landmark Friday Mosque with its distinctive minaret.
Riyadha Mosque
The spiritual heart of Lamu's Islamic scholarship since 1901, epicenter of the famous Maulidi festival that draws pilgrims from across East Africa.
Swahili House Museum
A beautifully restored 18th-century home revealing traditional Swahili domestic life, from plasterwork niches to the private courtyard and bridal chamber.
German Post Office Museum
A curious relic of 1888 when Germany ran its East African mail through Lamu, preserved with period documents and colonial-era photographs.
Lamu Donkey Sanctuary
A waterfront refuge caring for injured and elderly working donkeys, central to daily life on car-free Lamu Island, open for visits and donations.
Harambee Avenue
Lamu's seafront promenade where dhows dock and fishermen mend sails at sunset, lined with the benches and porches that anchor the town's social life.

train.note: There is no railway on the Lamu archipelago or anywhere on Kenya's north coast - the SGR (https://metickets.krc.co.ke/) runs only between Mombasa and Nairobi. Lamu is reached by flying into Manda airstrip and taking a short boat across, or by road to Mokowe and then a boat.

bus.note: No international coaches. Buses run from Mombasa and Malindi to Mokowe on the mainland, taking about 6-8 hours from Mombasa, from where you cross by boat - there is no road onto Lamu island. Check current security advice for the Lamu County road, which has been subject to restrictions and convoy requirements in the past.

intl.to: Mokowe mainland jetty & Manda airstrip (Kenya) - motorised dhow, ~20-30 min
intl.op: local boat operators — tickets at the jetty
local dhow operators — arranged at the waterfront

ferry.note: There are no international sailings, but boats are the only transport here - Lamu town has almost no motor vehicles and no road bridge, so every arrival and departure is by water. The crossings from Mokowe and from Manda airstrip take twenty to thirty minutes in a motorised dhow, and services run to meet flights. Sailing dhows to Shela and the outer islands are hired by the trip.

half.name: Matondoni Village
half.blurb: A traditional boatbuilding village on Lamu island's western shore where craftsmen still construct and repair wooden dhows entirely by hand.

half.name: Takwa Ruins (Manda Island)
half.blurb: The atmospheric remains of a 16th-century Swahili trading town abandoned to baobabs, reached by dhow across the channel at high tide.
